01 — The case

A 36 W power board with more through-hole parts than any mounter can handle

The board is a 36 W power assembly for smart-home equipment, built 1×2 panelised on paper-phenolic substrate. Its insertion list holds 16 component types and 20 parts per panel — terminals, sockets, optocouplers, safety capacitors, TRIACs, electrolytics, fuse holders, inductors, transformers. Before this project every one of those leads was pushed by hand, then the panel moved to a hand-insertion bench that set its own pace, its own clinch angle and its own defect rate.

Verified — customer case deck (anonymised)
01

The brief

Replace manual insertion for everything that can be automated, keep the line balanced at one board every 9 seconds, and clinch every part that has to survive the wave solder without lifting. Board edge at least 5 mm, hole diameter at least 0.5 mm, body spacing at least 2 mm — all met by the customer design.

02

The audit

We mapped every part to a feeder family and a station, exactly the way the colour-coded panel analysis shows: green, blue, purple, yellow and dark-blue parts go to machines one to five. The red-marked parts — secondary-processed pieces that deform easily — were deliberately left on the manual bench. That decision is in the deck, and it stays on this page.

03

The answer

Three 4-head odd-form inserters (0.4–0.6 s per part) plus two gantry vision inserters (1–2 s per part), SMEMA-linked with a magazine loader and unloader around a wave solder. Corner clinching on the parts that need it; no clinch on fuse holders, the inductor and the transformer.

The line is a single file of SMEMA-linked stations: the magazine loader presents the panel, five odd-form inserters take their slice of the part list, the wave solder completes the joints, and the unloader stacks the finished panels. Total length in this configuration: 15,790 mm.

03 — Why automate

Twenty hand-inserted leads per panel is a cost that never graduates

Hand insertion looks cheap because it is paid by the month, not by the board. This case removes 20 leads per panel from the bench — and with them the variance that walks in with every shift change. The S7000-series platform performs the whole motion set — pick, centre, insert, clinch, and on the strip feeders even the cutting — at a fixed force and a fixed angle, 800 small boards an hour.

01

The bench scales with headcount, not demand

More orders means more insertion operators, more supervision and more re-training; fewer orders means idle benches. The line scales by program: change the part list and the teaching, keep the operators for what needs hands.

02

Wrong part and wrong polarity are silent until test

The bowls check orientation and the tube and tape feeders key the part the only way it fits; the gantry cameras re-find the hole on every board. In this case the deck lists direction detection as a machine function — the bench has no equivalent.

03

A lifted lead at the wave costs three times

A part that floats during soldering is a rework, a risk and a scrap candidate. Corner clinching — the base rising with the insertion and the circuit confirming the bend — is what keeps 20 parts seated through the wave at 9 seconds a panel.

04 — The machines

Two platforms, one insertion family

Stations 1 to 3 are the 4-head odd-form platform: servo axes, cam-driven material clamp, vacuum locating, programmable insertion direction. Stations 4 and 5 are the gantry platform: dual-drive Y axis, three 500 W cameras and an electric gripper that adjusts width and force to the part. Both run the same programming model and the same feeder families.

What is inside the insertion cycle

Vacuum locating and cam clamp

The head picks the component, vacuum initial-locates it by body shape, and the electric cam-driven clamp holds the body while the push rod drives it down. The part is guided, never squeezed by feel.

V-groove lead guide

A V-groove guide device aligns the lead tips before entry, so the component finds the hole instead of hunting for it — the difference between an insertion and a bent lead.

Rising die with circuit detection

As the part enters, the bottom die rises with it, bends the leads and confirms the bend electrically through the detection circuit. No confirmation, no pass.

Clinch that survives linking

Corner clinching holds the part even when the next machine picks the panel a second later — the deck states it plainly: multi-machine linking would otherwise eject freshly inserted parts.

Gantry with dual-drive Y

The gantry platform drives Y from two servos for speed and stability at the 450 × 300 mm board envelope — the station type used here for fuse holders, the inductor and the transformer.

Three cameras, one electric gripper

Two 500 W cameras read the component leads, the third reads the PCB; the electric gripper adjusts its width and clamping force to the part size automatically.

Components we specify, not invent

Panasonic AC servos

Motion control by Panasonic servo controller and motors on every axis.

THK ballscrews

Imported THK precision ballscrews, 0.01 mm class, on the drive axes.

AirTAC and SMC

AirTAC cylinders and SMC solenoid valves as standard — parts your maintenance team can buy anywhere.

Industrial PC plus motion card

Self-developed control software on an industrial PC with a dedicated motion control card and a 17-inch colour display.

05 — Feeding

The feeder is the machine

Every odd-form project is decided by how your parts arrive. This case runs four of the five feeder families on one line — reel, bowl, tube and tape — and the tray family is waiting in the wings for the next board. Each family is a Southern-designed unit, not an adapter bolted to someone else's assumption.

Vibratory bowl feeders

For bulk parts: sockets, safety capacitors, TRIACs, electrolytics, inductors, transformers. The bowl orients and inspects direction and appearance before the part is presented — bad orientations recirculate instead of travelling.

Taped feeders

For components on tape at pitches from 2.5 to 15 mm — 2.5, 3.5, 5.0, 7.5, 10, 15 mm. The vertical feeder keys polarity mechanically and the insertion rate stays high because the part is already positioned.

Tube magazines

For tubed parts — optocouplers and relays in this case. The tube defines polarity and position by geometry alone, and the packaging is reusable.

Tray magazines

For blister and tray-packed parts — tray ICs, tubed amplifiers, parts that hate being tumbled. The tray is presented to the head; nothing vibrates.

Reel and strip feeders

For 187 and 250 faston terminals on linked strip or reel, with the cutting knife built into the feeder. The two terminal standards run on the same unit — the case's first station lives on this feeder.

06 — The 9 seconds

Where the 9 seconds per panel go

Every station gets the same budget: 3 s of insertion, 3 s of board transfer, 3 s of load and unload — 9 s per panel end to end, and because the stations are balanced, the line runs at that rhythm. On the 1×2 panel that is 400 panels an hour, 800 small boards an hour.

08 — Configuration

Options and equipment suggestions

Two lines with the same part list can cost very differently depending on six decisions. Make them with us before the quotation, not after.

Options quoted from platform documents

Head count and station split

1 to 4 heads on the odd-form platform, 2 on the gantry. One head is one component type per pass — the part list decides the machine count, not the catalogue.

Feeder family per part

Bowl, tape, tube, tray or reel. Where a part exists in two packages, we price both and tell you which one saves money over a year of reels.

Clinch strategy

Corner clinch for parts that must survive the wave, no clinch where the joint or a secondary process forbids it, lead clinch where the deck calls for it. Mixed on the same line is normal.

Board handling

Standalone machines, or SMEMA-linked with magazine loader, conveyors and unloader as in this case. Envelope from 100 × 100 mm up to 380 × 280 mm (4-head) or 450 × 300 mm (gantry), enlarged on request.

Vision and detection

Mark-point correction, lead cameras and PCB camera on the gantry platform, direction and appearance inspection at the bowl. The level of checking is a configuration, not a guess.

Programming and data

Online visual programming with image correction, Excel-style part tables, USB import. Ask about the array-data and automatic-learning options if you run many similar boards.

09 — Installation

What your floor needs before the first panel

The case line went from delivery to balanced running in days, not weeks, because the utilities were ready. Here is the checklist we send with every line.

STEP 1

Space and levelling

15.8 m of line length in this configuration, plus operator access on both sides. Level each machine on its feet before linking conveyors.

STEP 2

Power

Single-phase 220 V AC, 50/60 Hz, 2 kVA per insertion machine. Provide a clean, earthed supply per station.

STEP 3

Compressed air

5–6 kgf/cm² (about 0.5–0.6 MPa) regulated at the machine, roughly 0.6 m³/min consumption per inserter. Dry, clean air protects the valves and the clinch dies.

STEP 4

Environment

10–30 °C and 30–70 percent humidity, non-condensing — the range the platform manual states, and the range your solder joints will thank you for.

STEP 5

SMEMA linking

Loader, inserters, wave solder and unloader handshake over SMEMA signals. Confirm board flow direction and by-pass logic at layout stage.

STEP 6

First-article programming

We teach the first board with your process engineer at the machine — marks, pickup positions, block data — and hand over the program file with the acceptance report.

ARTICLE 01The 20-part board that made the insertion bench the bottleneck

A four-step audit that turns a hand-insertion bench into a number you can defend — with the red-marked parts left honestly on the bench.

Articles are marketing commentary. Machine facts quoted inside them come from the customer case deck, the S-7000 platform manual and the S7900 2025 catalogue; full text in English.

There is a line on this customer's panel that never made it into a meeting: twenty through-hole leads per panel, all of them pushed by hand, all of them on the critical path of a product the factory sells by the megawatt.

Look at the shape of the cost. A manual THT bench pays every month, re-trains every product change and re-qualifies every resignation. The panel in this case has 16 component types — faston strips, sockets, optocouplers, safety capacitors, TRIACs, electrolytics, fuse holders, an inductor and a transformer. Every one of those parts is a different feel in the operator's hand, and feel is exactly what your yield does not want.

Here is the audit we ran before proposing a single machine. One: list every through-hole part with its package — bulk, taped, tube, tray, strip. Two: mark each part with the holes it needs: hole at least 0.5 mm, board edge at least 5 mm, body spacing at least 2 mm, lead deformation under 0.1 mm. Three: colour-code the panel by machine — in this case five colours, five stations. Four: mark in red the parts that should stay manual. That fourth step is the one most vendors skip.

The answer was a line of five S7000-series odd-form inserters — three 4-head machines and two gantry vision machines — SMEMA-linked with a magazine loader and a wave solder across 15,790 mm. The parts that must survive the wave get corner clinching from a rising die with electrical confirmation. The result on the customer's own arithmetic: 9 seconds a panel, 800 small boards an hour.

Once the bench is gone the numbers keep working. The insertion cost per board becomes a figure you can put inside a quotation. The freed operators absorb the product changes that used to need re-training. And the red-marked parts? They stay where they are safest — which is precisely why the rest of the line can be trusted.

Run the four-step audit on your own board and send it to info@smthelp.com or on WhatsApp at +86 13602562576. We will return a colour-coded station plan and a payback figure with your numbers — the same arithmetic, no brochure attached.

ARTICLE 02No wrong parts, no wrong polarity: what the machine actually guarantees

Detection is a mechanism, not a mood — how orientation checks, keyed feeders and a circuit-confirmed clinch remove the silent defects.

Articles are marketing commentary. Machine facts quoted inside them come from the customer case deck, the S-7000 platform manual and the S7900 2025 catalogue; full text in English.

Every EMS manager says two sentences out loud about through-hole insertion. One: it is not that hard. Two: we cannot find people who do it. Both are true, and the second one is getting louder.

The hard part of hand insertion is not any single lead — it is the variance. A socket seated at a slight angle passes the bench and fails the wave. An optocoupler rotated 180 degrees passes the wave and fails test. A faston strip pushed with a heavy thumb deforms the terminal and deforms the schedule. None of it is visible until it is expensive.

The fix is not a better operator. It is a machine that refuses to be wrong: bowls that inspect orientation and appearance before a part is presented, tubes and tape that key the part the only way it fits, a V-groove guide that aligns the lead tips before entry, and a rising bottom die that bends the leads and confirms the bend through a detection circuit. No confirmation, no pass — that is the whole philosophy.

The case on this page runs exactly that stack: vacuum locating, cam-driven clamp, electric push, circuit-checked clinch on every part that needs it, and on the gantry stations, three cameras that re-find the hole on every board instead of trusting nominal coordinates. The deck's own words for it: no wrong parts, no wrong polarity — because wrong is detected, not hoped against.

And the loop closes where quality lives. Once insertion is confirmed electrically, your test station stops finding polarity escapes, your rework rate stops being a mystery, and your audits stop needing an operator-hero story. Quality becomes a machine property, which means it repeats.

Send your part list and one of your worst defect reports to info@smthelp.com — we will tell you which of your parts the detection stack would catch, and which it would not.

ARTICLE 03The feeder decision nobody talks about

Bowl, tape, tube, tray or reel: the quiet choice that decides whether your odd-form line runs at its rating.

Articles are marketing commentary. Machine facts quoted inside them come from the customer case deck, the S-7000 platform manual and the S7900 2025 catalogue; full text in English.

Buyers spend their evaluation on the insertion head. They spend their money on the feeder.

It is the quiet decision in every odd-form project. The head is the same disciplined mechanism all day; the feeder is what decides whether your part arrives oriented, damaged, late or never. Yet most quotations treat feeders as accessories, and most lines are born bottlenecked.

There are five families, and the part list picks them. Vibratory bowls for bulk parts — with direction and appearance inspection at the bowl, so bad orientations recirculate instead of travelling. Taped feeders for components on tape, at pitches from 2.5 to 15 mm, polarity keyed mechanically. Tube magazines for tubed parts like the optocouplers in this case — geometry alone guarantees orientation. Tray magazines for parts that hate being tumbled. Reel and strip feeders with built-in cutting for 187 and 250 faston terminals — the two standards run on the same unit.

This case line runs four of the five families at once: reel and bowl on station 1, tube and bowl on station 2, bowl and tape on station 3, tape on station 4, bowl on station 5. That is the real specification of the line — not heads, but feeders, and the station plan that assigns every part to the right one.

The feeder decision compounds: the same bowl serves the next product with a new tooling plate; the same tape family covers your electrolytics and your fuse holders; the packaging you save on — bulk instead of tape, reusable tubes — is a line item in your BOM forever.

Tell us how your parts arrive — bulk, taped, tubed, tray, reel — and we will send back the feeder assignment for your board, with the cost of each family marked.

ARTICLE 04Nine seconds a panel: how a THT line is actually timed

The station-split arithmetic behind a balanced line, taken straight from the case deck.

Articles are marketing commentary. Machine facts quoted inside them come from the customer case deck, the S-7000 platform manual and the S7900 2025 catalogue; full text in English.

Ninety seconds is roughly what a panel spent on the manual bench in this case. Nine seconds is what it spends on the line. The difference is not speed — it is timing.

Manual benches do not have a takt; they have a mood. The line in this case has a heartbeat so regular you can set a watch by it: 3 s of insertion, 3 s of transfer, 3 s of load and unload, at every station, every panel. When all five stations share the same 9-second budget, the line is balanced — and a balanced line is the only kind that delivers its theoretical number.

How do you get there? The deck shows the arithmetic, and you should run it on your own board. For each station: insertion time per part times the number of parts, plus board transfer, plus load and unload. The slowest station sets the pace, so the part list is split across machines until every station lands on the same budget. In this case: 6 parts at 0.5 s, 6 at 0.5 s, 3 at 1 s, 3 at 1 s, 2 at 1.5 s — five stations, one rhythm. The panel is 1×2, so 400 panels an hour reads as 800 small boards an hour.

The machines that hold that rhythm are built for it: servo axes with 0.001 mm resolution, a cam-driven clamp that grips by geometry, a rising die that moves with the part instead of against it, and a gantry with dual-drive Y that does not slow down at 450 × 300 mm. The 9 seconds is a design target the hardware was chosen to meet.

Once the rhythm exists, everything else hangs on it: the wave solder stops waiting for boards, the loader stops being a person, and your schedule becomes a multiplication problem. Lines that run at a heartbeat are the lines that go lights-out next.

Send us your part list and your current per-panel insertion time. We will return the station split and the takt calculation — the same table the deck used, with your numbers.

ARTICLE 05When not to automate: the parts we left on the bench

The most credible page in the deck is the one with red marks — the four-bucket map that keeps deformed parts off the machines.

Articles are marketing commentary. Machine facts quoted inside them come from the customer case deck, the S-7000 platform manual and the S7900 2025 catalogue; full text in English.

The most credible page in this customer's deck is not the machine photo. It is the panel analysis with red marks on it.

Because the red marks say: these parts stay manual. Secondary-processed pieces that deform easily — a bent lead here, a crushed tab there — are not automation failures, they are automation candidates that would cost more to automate than to insert. A vendor who promises you 100 percent is a vendor who has not looked at your board.

The honest framework is a four-bucket map. Bucket one: parts with straight physics — terminals, sockets, capacitors — to the 4-head platform, 0.4 to 0.6 s a part. Bucket two: parts that need the camera and the electric gripper — fuse holders, the inductor, the transformer — to the gantry stations. Bucket three: parts that need clinching to survive the wave, marked with the clinch type. Bucket four: the red parts, which go to a small bench at the end of the line and stay there.

That map is the deliverable. The five S7000-series machines are what this customer's map produced — but the same method on your board may produce two machines, or seven, or a line where the transformer is inserted and the heat-sink tab is not. We publish the platform manuals and the design guideline precisely so you can run the map yourself first.

The red marks also protect the line. A deformed part jamming a bowl feeder at 0.5 s a piece turns nine seconds a panel into a fifteen-minute recovery. Keeping the wrong parts off the machine is what lets the right parts run at the machine's rating, day after day.

If a vendor promises to insert everything, send us the parts they promised. We will tell you, free and in writing, which ones belong on the bench — and price the ones that do not.

ARTICLE 06Clinch or don't: the decision that shows up at the wave solder

Why corner clinching is what turns five machines in a row into one line — and which parts in this case run without it.

Articles are marketing commentary. Machine facts quoted inside them come from the customer case deck, the S-7000 platform manual and the S7900 2025 catalogue; full text in English.

There is a moment in every THT line where a part decides whether it is going to the customer or to rework. That moment is the wave solder.

A part that sat politely on the manual bench can still float when the panel meets molten solder — steam from the flux pushes up under the body and the unsecured part lifts, bridges, or walks out of the hole. The defect is not born at insertion. It is born at the wave, and it is paid for at test.

The prevention is mechanical and it is decided part by part. Corner clinching: as the part enters, the bottom die rises with it, bends the leads at the corners and confirms the bend through a detection circuit. The deck adds the detail that matters for linked lines — without clinching, the next machine picking the panel a second later can eject freshly inserted parts. Clinching is what makes a line a line instead of five machines standing in a row.

In this case the decision is visible station by station. Terminals, sockets, optocouplers, safety capacitors, TRIACs and electrolytics: corner clinch. Fuse holders, the inductor, the transformer: no clinch — the joint or a secondary process does not want it. Two platforms do the split: the 4-head machines with the rising die, the gantry machines with camera-verified placement and an electric gripper that adjusts force to the part.

The clinch decision is also a cost decision, and it repeats. A clinched part that survives the wave is one fewer panel in the rework queue; a part that needs no clinch is one fewer die to maintain. The station plan prices both honestly, and the documents on this page are the same ones our engineers quote from.

Tell us which of your parts lift at the wave today. We will show you what the rising die does to that list — and which parts we would leave unclinched, with the reason.

ARTICLE 07From part list to running line: the four gates

Feasibility map, configuration drawing, sample insertion, training — the honest path this case walked in weeks.

Articles are marketing commentary. Machine facts quoted inside them come from the customer case deck, the S-7000 platform manual and the S7900 2025 catalogue; full text in English.

Nobody signs a fifteen-metre line on the first call. The honest path from a part list to a running line has four gates, and this case walked all of them.

The fear at gate one is real: a line is capital, and capital deserves a documented decision. The old way was a sales visit and a promise. The new way is arithmetic at every gate — and the customer keeps the arithmetic either way.

Gate one: the feasibility map. You send the part list, board dimensions and current insertion time; we send back the colour-coded panel — every part assigned a station, a feeder family and a clinch decision, red marks included. Gate two: the configuration sheet and layout drawing — head counts, feeder assignment, SMEMA flow, the 15,790 mm of this case, utilities marked: 220 V single-phase 2 kVA per inserter, 5–6 kgf/cm² air, 0.6 m³ per minute. Gate three: sample insertion on your own boards, on our floor, with a report you can circulate internally. Gate four: delivery, installation to the checklist on this page, and first-article programming trained at the machine with your engineer.

The machines at the end of that path are not a mystery box: Panasonic servos, THK ballscrews, AirTAC and SMC pneumatic components, a 17-inch display and self-developed software — all specified in the platform manual, so your maintenance team knows what it owns before it buys it.

Each gate is a decision point with a cost of passing and a cost of stopping. Factories that run the gates in order stop at gate one when they should, and ship at gate four when they should. The case on this page ran its gates in weeks.

Start at gate one — it is free. Send the part list to info@smthelp.com and get the station plan with the red marks.

ARTICLE 08What 800 boards an hour does to your quotations

Stable insertion cost per board is a pricing weapon — the bench variance it removes, priced with your wage.

Articles are marketing commentary. Machine facts quoted inside them come from the customer case deck, the S-7000 platform manual and the S7900 2025 catalogue; full text in English.

The sales team does not think about the insertion bench. The insertion bench is the reason the sales team loses.

Because every hand-inserted lead is a cost that moves: wages move, the yield moves with the shift, the lead time moves with the calendar. A quotation built on bench numbers is a quotation you cannot defend twice — and in EMS, the second time is where the margin lives.

Fix the insertion cost and the whole quotation stabilises. Twenty leads per panel at machine rates — 0.5 s on the 4-head stations, 1 to 1.5 s on the gantry — turns the bench's variable cost into a line's fixed cost: depreciation, one operator, electricity. The number per board stops moving, which means the number in the quotation stops being a hope.

The case on this page is the worked example: 16 part types, 20 parts per panel, five S7000-series inserters, 9 seconds a panel, 800 small boards an hour. Put your wage and your volume beside those numbers with the calculator above and the arithmetic is yours — not ours. The same page also shows what the line does not do: the red-marked parts, priced honestly on the bench.

And the stable number compounds. A quotation you can defend becomes orders you can schedule; a schedule you can keep becomes the customer who stops asking for a second price. The bench was never the cost problem — the variance was.

Send your boards-per-day and your loaded wage. We will send back the insertion cost per board with the machine numbers and the manual numbers, separated — the same table style as this case.

15 — FAQ

Answers to the questions this case raises

Which components can an odd-form inserter actually place?
Anything with leads that fits the physics: relays, transformers, optocouplers, sockets, faston terminals (187 and 250 on strip), safety and electrolytic capacitors, TRIACs, fuse holders, inductors, eyelets, tact switches. This case places 16 types in one line. The limits are honest: lead deformation under 0.1 mm, hole diameter at least 0.5 mm, board edge at least 5 mm, body spacing at least 2 mm.
Can it handle my board size?
The case deck specifies up to 380 × 280 mm on the 4-head platform and 450 × 300 mm on the gantry, minimum 100 × 100 mm, with enlarged sizes on request; the S-7000 platform document lists up to 480 × 390 mm for some configurations. Both numbers are published on this page — send us your panel and we will tell you which envelope applies.
Which parts get clinched and which do not?
Parts that must survive the wave without lifting get corner clinching — in this case the terminals, sockets, optocouplers, capacitors and TRIACs. Fuse holders, the inductor and the transformer run without clinch. The decision is made part by part in the station plan, and the deck that designed this line shows it.
My parts come bulk / taped / tubed / on trays / on reels — what feeds them?
Five feeder families cover all of it: vibratory bowls with direction and appearance inspection, taped feeders at 2.5 to 15 mm pitches, tube magazines, tray magazines and reel or strip feeders with built-in cutting for 187 and 250 terminals. Mixed families on one line is the normal case, not the exception.
How long does programming and changeover take?
Programming is online visual teaching with image correction, or Excel-style part tables imported over USB. A changeover is a program load plus a feeder swap — which is why the station plan assigns parts to heads by family, not by accident. Ask about array data and automatic learning for families of similar boards.
How was 800 boards an hour calculated?
From the deck: each station spends 3 s inserting, 3 s transferring and 3 s loading — 9 s per panel; on the 1×2 panel that is 400 panels, 800 small boards per hour, and the line runs balanced at the slowest station. Your number comes from your part list, and we show you the arithmetic the same way.
Should every part be automated?
No. The parts this deck marks red — secondary-processed pieces that deform easily — stay on the manual bench on purpose. A line plan that automates 20 of 23 parts and tells you the truth about the other three beats one that promises everything.
What happens after I send my part list?
You get a feasibility map like the colour-coded panel analysis on this page — every part assigned a station, a feeder and a clinch decision — then a configuration sheet, a layout drawing and a quotation. Sample insertion on your own boards is available before you commit.
